slides.narration: Physics is a science of measurement. A bowler measures speed, an engineer measures strain on a bridge, an astronomer measures the distance to a star, and each needs a number and a unit. In this part we study systems of units, the international system and its rules, the prefixes, and the practical units that stretch from a nucleus to a galaxy.

slides.heading: A unit is a reference standard
slides.body_md: To measure is to compare with a standard of the same kind. The result is **number × unit**; the number alone says nothing.
bullets: **Fundamental (base) quantities** such as length, mass and time are chosen independently; every other quantity is **derived** from them.
The standard chosen for a quantity is its **unit**; a good unit is well defined, reproducible, invariable and convenient.
Changing the unit changes the number but not the physical quantity: $n_1 u_1 = n_2 u_2$.

rows: its size is stated without ambiguity
anyone, anywhere, can set up the same standard
it does not change with time, place or temperature
of a size that suits the measurement, with prefixes for the rest

visual.alt: Table of the four properties of a good unit: well defined, reproducible, invariable and convenient

slides.narration: To measure something is to compare it with a standard of the same kind. The answer is a number times a unit, and the number alone means nothing. A good standard is well defined, reproducible by anyone, invariable with time and place, and of a convenient size. If we change the unit the number changes, but the quantity itself stays exactly the same.

slides.heading: Systems of units: CGS, FPS, MKS, MKSA and SI
slides.body_md: A **system of units** fixes the units of the base quantities; all other units follow from them.
bullets: **CGS** uses centimetre, gram, second; **FPS** uses foot, pound, second; **MKS** uses metre, kilogram, second.
**MKSA** adds the ampere for electric current. The **SI** (Système International) extends MKSA to seven base units and is now used worldwide.
Force is a dyne in CGS, a poundal in FPS and a newton in MKS and SI.

visual.alt: Table of the CGS, FPS, MKS, MKSA and SI systems of units with the units of length, mass, time, force and work in each

slides.narration: Different systems choose different base units. The C G S system uses centimetre, gram and second. The F P S system uses foot, pound and second. The M K S system uses metre, kilogram and second, and M K S A adds the ampere for current. The S I extends this to seven base units and is used all over the world. The unit of force is the dyne, the poundal or the newton, depending on the system.

slides.heading: The seven SI base units
slides.body_md: The SI has **seven** base quantities. Since 2019 each unit is defined by fixing a constant of nature.
bullets: The **metre** follows from fixing the speed of light, $c = 299\,792\,458$ m s$^{-1}$, and the **second** from the frequency of a caesium atomic clock.
The **kilogram** is fixed through the Planck constant; the **ampere** through the elementary charge.
The **kelvin**, **mole** and **candela** are fixed through the Boltzmann constant, the Avogadro constant and a defined luminous efficacy.

visual.alt: Table of the seven SI base quantities with their units and symbols

slides.narration: The S I has seven base units: metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin, mole and candela. Since two thousand nineteen each one is tied to a constant of nature. For example, the speed of light is fixed at exactly two hundred and ninety nine million, seven hundred and ninety two thousand, four hundred and fifty eight metres per second, and that fixes the metre.

slides.heading: Derived units
slides.body_md: Every other SI unit is **derived** by multiplying or dividing base units. Many have special names.
bullets: One newton is the force that gives a mass of 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m s$^{-2}$.
Rewriting a named unit in base units is a quick way to check an answer.

visual.alt: Table of derived quantities, their named SI units and the same units written in base units

slides.narration: A derived unit is a product or quotient of base units. Force is mass times acceleration, so the newton is one kilogram metre per second squared. The joule, watt, pascal, hertz and coulomb are also names for particular combinations. Rewriting a named unit in base units is a good way to check a result.

slides.heading: Supplementary units: radian and steradian
slides.body_md: Earlier the radian and steradian were called **supplementary units**; today they are **dimensionless derived units**.
bullets: **Plane angle:** $\theta = \dfrac{s}{r}$; one radian $= \dfrac{180^\circ}{\pi} \approx 57.3^\circ$.
**Solid angle:** $\Omega = \dfrac{A}{r^2}$; a whole sphere subtends $4\pi$ steradian.

slides.narration: To measure an angle, draw a circle about its tip. The angle in radians is the arc divided by the radius. When the arc equals the radius the angle is one radian, about fifty seven point three degrees. The solid angle is the area of a patch on the sphere divided by the radius squared, in steradians. Both are ratios of like quantities, so neither has dimensions.

slides.heading: Rules for writing unit names and symbols
slides.body_md: The SI has fixed rules so that a measurement reads the same everywhere:
bullets: Write a product of units with a space, as in N m, and a quotient with a negative power, as in m s$^{-1}$.
Use at most one solidus: write m s$^{-2}$ rather than m/s/s.

rows: names are lower case, even when named after a person
a symbol is capital only if the unit is named after a person
no full stop after a symbol (except at the end of a sentence)
a space between the number and the symbol
do not mix names and symbols
one prefix only, joined to the unit

slides.narration: Here are the rules. Unit names are written in lower case, even when named after a person, so newton and kelvin. A symbol is a capital only when the unit is named after a person. Symbols are never made plural, take no full stop, and stand a space after the number. Never mix names and symbols, and never stack two prefixes on one unit.

slides.heading: SI prefixes from atto to tera
slides.body_md: A **prefix** multiplies the unit it is joined to by a power of ten. Never join two prefixes.
bullets: Most prefixes go in steps of 1000; centi, deci, deca and hecto are the exceptions.
The kilogram is the only base unit whose name carries a prefix; prefixes for mass are added to the gram, as in $1\ \mu\text{g} = 10^{-9}$ kg.

visual.alt: Table of the SI prefixes from atto to tera with their symbols and powers of ten

slides.narration: Prefixes keep numbers readable. Kilo is a thousand, mega a million, giga a thousand million and tera a million million. Going down, milli is a thousandth, micro a millionth, nano a thousand millionth, then pico, femto and atto. Centi, deci, deca and hecto are the odd ones out, not in steps of a thousand. The kilogram is the only base unit with a prefix, so mass prefixes are added to the gram.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: prefixes and derived units
slides.body_md: Express in SI base units without prefixes: (a) a train speed of 270 km h$^{-1}$; (b) a capacitance of 2.2 μF; (c) a clock rate of 4.2 GHz; (d) the pascal.
bullets: (d) pressure $=$ force ÷ area, so 1 Pa $= \dfrac{\text{kg m s}^{-2}}{\text{m}^2} = kg m⁻¹ s⁻²$.

visual.alt: Table of the SI prefixes from atto to tera with their symbols and powers of ten

slides.narration: For part a, multiply by one thousand metres and divide by three thousand six hundred seconds to get 75.0 metres per second. In part b, micro means ten to the minus six. In part c, giga means ten to the nine. In part d, pressure is force over area, so the pascal is kilogram per metre per second squared.

slides.heading: Practical units for the very large and the very small
slides.body_md: SI units are awkward at the extremes, so physicists also use **practical units**:
bullets: A **light year** is the distance light travels in a year: $2.998 \times 10^{8} \times 3.156 \times 10^{7} \approx 9.46 \times 10^{15}$ m.
The **astronomical unit** is the mean Earth–Sun distance; the **parsec** is about 3.26 light years.
The **fermi** and **angstrom** suit nuclei and atoms; the **unified atomic mass unit** is one twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom.

rows: sizes of atoms, wavelengths of light

slides.narration: Distances between stars are far too large for metres, so astronomers use the light year, the distance light covers in a year, about 9.46 thousand million million metres. The astronomical unit is the Earth to Sun distance, and the parsec is about three point two six light years. For the tiny scale there are the angstrom, the fermi, and the unified atomic mass unit for the masses of atoms.

slides.heading: Parallax and the parsec
slides.body_md: The **parsec** comes from the **parallax** method: the angle $p$ that a baseline $b$ subtends at a distant object gives its distance.
bullets: For a small angle, $D = \dfrac{b}{p}$ with $p$ in radian.
One parsec is the distance at which the baseline of 1 AU subtends $p = 1$ arcsecond, so $1\ \text{pc} = \dfrac{1\ \text{AU}}{4.848 \times 10^{-6}} \approx 3.08 \times 10^{16}$ m.

slides.narration: Hold a finger at arm length and look with one eye, then the other: it seems to jump against the background. That shift is parallax. Astronomers use the baseline between the Earth and the Sun, one astronomical unit. The distance of a star is the baseline divided by its parallax angle in radians. A star whose parallax is one arcsecond lies one parsec away.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: distance from parallax
slides.body_md: A star has a parallax of 0.4 arcsecond against a baseline of 1 AU. Find its distance in parsec, in light year and in AU. (1 pc $= 3.08 \times 10^{16}$ m, 1 ly $= 9.46 \times 10^{15}$ m, 1 AU $= 1.496 \times 10^{11}$ m.)
bullets: Step 1 — by the definition of the parsec, $D = \dfrac{1}{p} = \dfrac{1}{0.4} = 2.50$ pc.
Step 2 — in metre: $2.50 \times 3.08 \times 10^{16} \approx 7.70 \times 10^{16}$ m.
Step 3 — in light year: $\dfrac{7.70 \times 10^{16}}{9.46 \times 10^{15}} \approx 8.14$ ly; in AU: $\dfrac{7.70 \times 10^{16}}{1.496 \times 10^{11}} \approx 5.15 \times 10^{5}$ AU.

slides.body_md: The method must suit the scale. Each step up or down in size needs a new technique.
bullets: **Length:** direct scales for everyday sizes, electron or X-ray methods for atoms, parallax and radar echoes for the Moon, planets and stars.
**Mass:** a balance for ordinary masses, a mass spectrometer for atoms, orbits and gravitation for planets and stars.
**Time:** pendulum and quartz clocks for ordinary times, atomic clocks for the highest precision.

slides.narration: No single instrument works at every scale. For lengths we use scales and callipers, then electron or X ray methods for atoms, and parallax or radar echoes for the Moon, planets and stars. For masses we use a balance, a mass spectrometer for atoms, and orbits and gravitation for planets. For time we use a pendulum or quartz clock, and an atomic clock for the greatest precision.

Unit names and symbols follow fixed rules, and prefixes run from atto to tera. Practical units such as the fermi, angstrom, astronomical unit, light year, parsec and atomic mass unit cover the very small and the very large, and parallax gives stellar distances.

slides.narration: Every measurement is a little uncertain. In this part we ask how large the error is, how many digits a result deserves, and how to estimate an order of magnitude. slides.heading: Errors in measurement
slides.body_md: **Accuracy** is closeness to the true value; **precision** is closeness of repeated readings to one another. Errors come in two main kinds.
bullets: **Systematic errors** push every reading the same way: zero error, a faulty scale, a wrong technique, an observer's habit.
**Random errors** scatter readings both ways and are reduced by averaging many readings.
The **least count** is the smallest division the instrument shows and limits any single reading.

visual.alt: Table of systematic, random and least-count errors with causes, effects and remedies

slides.narration: Accuracy means closeness to the true value, and precision means that repeated readings agree with one another. Systematic errors, such as a zero error or a worn scale, push every reading the same way. Random errors scatter the readings both ways, and averaging many readings reduces them. The least count of the instrument sets a limit for any single reading.

slides.heading: Absolute, relative and percentage error
slides.body_md: With repeated readings $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$ of the same quantity:
bullets: The **mean** is the best estimate of the true value.
The **absolute error** of a reading is its difference from the mean; the **mean absolute error** is the average of these.
The **relative error** is the mean absolute error divided by the mean; the **percentage error** is that times 100 %.

slides.heading: Significant figures and how to count them
slides.body_md: A measured value shows the digits the instrument gives **certainly**, plus **one uncertain** digit estimated by eye. Together they are its **significant figures**.
bullets: The strip on the millimetre scale reads 5.27 cm: 5 and 2 are certain, the last digit 7 is an estimate, so there are 3 significant figures.
Changing the unit must not change the count; writing $a \times 10^{n}$ removes any doubt about trailing zeros.

rows: Zeros before the first non-zero digit do not count
Trailing zeros after a decimal point count
Trailing zeros with no decimal point do not count
Powers of ten do not count

visual.alt: Table of the rules for counting significant figures with an example and the count for each

slides.narration: A reading has the digits the instrument shows for certain and one estimated digit, and all of them are significant. Here are the rules. Every non zero digit counts. Zeros between non zero digits count. Zeros before the first non zero digit do not count, they only place the decimal point. Zeros at the end count when there is a decimal point and do not count when there is none. A power of ten never counts. Writing a number in scientific form removes any doubt.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: counting and rounding off
slides.body_md: State the number of significant figures in each value, then round each value in the second set to 3 significant figures.
bullets: Rounding off — if the digit to be dropped is more than 5, raise the last kept digit by one; if less than 5, leave it; if it is exactly 5 with nothing after it, make the last kept digit **even**.

rows: Zeros before the first non-zero digit do not count
Trailing zeros after a decimal point count
Trailing zeros with no decimal point do not count
Powers of ten do not count

visual.alt: Table of the rules for counting significant figures with an example and the count for each

slides.narration: First the counting. The first value has three, because the leading zeros do not count. The second has four, with the trailing zero after the decimal point. Twenty six hundred written without a decimal point has two, but in scientific form with a decimal it has four. For rounding, a dropped five leaves the last kept digit even, so seven point eight six five becomes seven point eight six, and seven point eight seven five becomes seven point eight eight.

slides.heading: Arithmetic with significant figures
slides.body_md: A calculator shows many digits; the answer may keep only as many as the data justify.
bullets: Carry **one extra digit** through intermediate steps and round only at the end.
Counted numbers and defined factors are **exact** and do not limit the answer.

rows: as many decimal places as the least precise number
as many significant figures as the least precise factor

visual.alt: Table of the rules for adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing with significant figures and for exact numbers

slides.narration: When adding or subtracting, look at decimal places: the answer keeps as many as the least precise number. When multiplying or dividing, look at significant figures: the answer keeps as many as the factor with the fewest. Exact numbers, such as the two wheels of a bicycle, never limit the answer. Round once, at the very end.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: calculations
slides.body_md: Evaluate with the correct number of significant figures: (a) $21.34 + 3.7 + 0.052$; (b) the area of a sheet $14.2$ cm by $6.35$ cm; (c) the speed of a trolley that covers $135$ m in $4.2$ s.
bullets: (a) The sum is $25.092$. The least precise number, $3.7$, has one decimal place, so the answer is $25.1$.
(b) $14.2 \times 6.35 = 90.17$ cm$^2$. Both factors have 3 significant figures, so the area is $90.2$ cm$^2$.
(c) $\dfrac{135}{4.2} = 32.14$. The factor $4.2$ has only 2 significant figures, so the speed is $32$ m s$^{-1}$.

slides.heading: Order of magnitude
slides.body_md: The **order of magnitude** of a number is the power of ten nearest to it. Write $N = a \times 10^{k}$ with $1 \le a < 10$.
bullets: If $a \le 3.16$ ($\sqrt{10}$) the order of magnitude is $10^{k}$; if $a > 3.16$ it is $10^{k+1}$.
It lets us compare sizes and make quick estimates: a result right to the order of magnitude is right to within a factor of about three.

slides.heading: Dimensions and dimensional formulae
slides.body_md: The **dimensions** of a quantity are the powers to which the base quantities, written $[\text{M}]$, $[\text{L}]$, $[\text{T}]$ and so on, appear in it. Its **dimensional formula** shows them, for example $[F] = [\text{M L T}^{-2}]$.
bullets: Pure numbers and ratios of like quantities, such as angle and strain, are dimensionless.
Dimensions follow from the defining relation; constants take the dimensions that make their equation balance.

visual.alt: Table of dimensional formulae of area, velocity, acceleration, momentum, force, energy, power, pressure, frequency and moment of inertia

slides.narration: The dimensions of a quantity show how the base quantities of mass, length and time enter it. Velocity is length over time, force is mass times length over time squared, and energy is mass times length squared over time squared. The table lists the dimensional formulae of the quantities you need. Pure numbers and ratios of like quantities have no dimensions.

slides.heading: Dimensions of physical constants
slides.body_md: A constant gets its dimensions from the equation in which it appears. For example $F = G m_1 m_2 / r^2$ gives $[G] = [F][r^2]/[m^2]$.
bullets: $[G] = [\mathrm{M}^{-1}\,\mathrm{L}^{3}\,\mathrm{T}^{-2}]$, $[h] = [\mathrm{M}\,\mathrm{L}^{2}\,\mathrm{T}^{-1}]$, $[k] = [\mathrm{M}\,\mathrm{T}^{-2}]$.
Many constants carry units that you must be able to write.

visual.alt: Table of the dimensional formulae of the gravitational constant, the Planck constant, the spring constant, surface tension, viscosity and the Boltzmann constant

slides.narration: A constant takes the dimensions that make its equation balance. From the law of gravitation, G equals force times distance squared over mass squared, so its dimensions are the inverse of mass times length cubed over time squared. The same method gives the dimensions of the Planck constant, the spring constant, surface tension and viscosity.

slides.heading: The principle of homogeneity
slides.body_md: **Principle of homogeneity:** every term on both sides of a correct physical equation has the same dimensions. Only like quantities can be added, subtracted or equated.
bullets: In $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$ every term has dimensions $[\text{L}^{2}\text{T}^{-2}]$.
The argument of sin, cos, log or an exponential must be dimensionless.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: checking equations
slides.body_md: Use dimensions to test the equations $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$, $P = \rho g h$, $K = \tfrac12 m v$ and $T = 2\pi\sqrt{l/g}$.
bullets: Find the dimensions of every term, using $[\rho] = [\text{ML}^{-3}]$, $[g] = [\text{LT}^{-2}]$ and so on.
If the terms agree, the equation is dimensionally consistent; if not, it is certainly wrong.
The kinetic energy formula fails: $[mv] = [\text{MLT}^{-1}]$, not the dimensions of energy.

visual.alt: Table checking four equations for dimensional consistency

slides.narration: For each equation we find the dimensions of every term. In v squared equals u squared plus two a s, all terms are length squared over time squared, so it passes. Pressure equals density times g times height balances. The period formula balances because the square root of length over g is a time. But half m v fails, since mass times velocity is momentum, not energy.

slides.heading: Converting units with dimensions
slides.body_md: If a quantity has dimensions $[\text{M}^{a}\text{L}^{b}\text{T}^{c}]$ and numerical value $n_1$ in a system with units $M_1, L_1, T_1$, its value in another system is
bullets: A larger unit gives a smaller number, so the ratio of units appears with the powers of the dimensions.

visual.alt: Table converting a newton, a joule, a pascal and an acceleration of 9.8 metres per second squared into CGS or FPS units using dimensions

slides.narration: To change systems, multiply the number by the ratio of the old unit to the new unit for each base quantity, each raised to the power in the dimensional formula. A larger unit gives a smaller number. The table shows the newton as one hundred thousand dynes, the joule as ten million ergs, and the acceleration of free fall in feet per second squared.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: converting and finding constants
slides.body_md: (a) Convert $G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}$ N m$^2$ kg$^{-2}$ to CGS units. (b) In the equation $\left(P + \dfrac{a}{V^2}\right)(V - b) = RT$ find the dimensions of $a$.
bullets: (a) $[G] = [\mathrm{M}^{-1}\,\mathrm{L}^{3}\,\mathrm{T}^{-2}]$: $n_2 = 6.67\times 10^{-11}\left(\dfrac{1\ \text{kg}}{1\ \text{g}}\right)^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1\ \text{m}}{1\ \text{cm}}\right)^{3} = 6.67\times 10^{-11}\times 10^{-3}\times 10^{6} = 6.67 \times 10^{-8}$ in CGS units.
(b) $a/V^2$ must have the dimensions of $P$, so $[a] = [P][V^2] = [\mathrm{M}\,\mathrm{L}^{-1}\,\mathrm{T}^{-2}][\text{L}^{6}] = [\mathrm{M}\,\mathrm{L}^{5}\,\mathrm{T}^{-2}]$.

visual.alt: Table converting a newton, a joule, a pascal and an acceleration of 9.8 metres per second squared into CGS or FPS units using dimensions

slides.narration: For part a, the gravitational constant has dimensions of inverse mass, length cubed, time to the minus two. Converting from kilogram and metre to gram and centimetre multiplies by ten to the minus three and by ten to the six, giving about 6.67 times ten to the minus eight in C G S units. For part b, a over V squared must have the dimensions of pressure, so a has the dimensions of pressure times length to the sixth power.

slides.heading: Limitations of dimensional analysis
slides.body_md: Dimensional analysis is a useful check, but it has limits:
bullets: It **cannot** give pure numbers or dimensionless constants such as $\tfrac12$ or $2\pi$.
It **cannot** handle sin, cos, log or exponential of a quantity with dimensions, nor derive a relation that has a sum of terms.
A dimensionally correct equation is **not necessarily correct**, and quantities with the same dimensions (work and torque) cannot be told apart.

rows: show that an equation is dimensionally wrong
prove that a dimensionally correct equation is right
give the dimensions of a constant in an equation
give pure numbers such as ½ or 2π
convert a quantity from one system of units to another
handle sin, log or exponential of a quantity with dimensions, or tell scalars from vectors

visual.alt: Table of what dimensional analysis can and cannot do

slides.narration: Dimensional analysis can show that an equation is wrong, but it cannot show that an equation is right. It cannot give pure numbers such as one half or two pi. It cannot deal with sines, logarithms or exponentials of a dimensional quantity, nor with a relation made of a sum of terms. And it cannot distinguish quantities with the same dimensions, like work and torque.

sections.heading: 1. Physics as measurement; units and systems of units
sections.body_md:
- Physics is built on **measurement**: a measured value is a **number × unit**. The unit is a **reference standard** of the same kind as the quantity.
- A good unit is **well defined, reproducible, invariable and convenient**. Changing the unit changes the number, not the quantity: $n_1u_1 = n_2u_2$.
- **Fundamental (base) quantities** are chosen independently; **derived quantities** are built from them.
- **Systems of units:** CGS (cm, g, s; force dyne, work erg), FPS (ft, lb, s; poundal), MKS (m, kg, s; newton, joule), **MKSA** (MKS plus the ampere) and the **SI**, which has seven base units and is used worldwide.
- Conversions used often: $1\ \text{N} = 10^{5}$ dyne, $1\ \text{J} = 10^{7}$ erg.

sections.heading: 2. SI base, supplementary and derived units; rules and prefixes
sections.body_md:
- **Seven SI base units:** metre (m), kilogram (kg), second (s), ampere (A), kelvin (K), mole (mol), candela (cd). Since 2019 each is defined by fixing a constant of nature (for example $c = 299\,792\,458$ m s$^{-1}$ fixes the metre).
- **Supplementary units** (now dimensionless derived units): **radian** ($\theta = s/r$) and **steradian** ($\Omega = A/r^2$). A circle is $2\pi$ rad; a sphere $4\pi$ sr; $1\ \text{rad} \approx 57.3^\circ$.
- **Derived units** such as newton $= \text{kg m s}^{-2}$, joule $= \text{kg m}^2\text{s}^{-2}$, watt $= \text{kg m}^2\text{s}^{-3}$, pascal $= \text{kg m}^{-1}\text{s}^{-2}$, hertz $= \text{s}^{-1}$, coulomb $= \text{A s}$.
- **Rules:** unit names in lower case; a symbol is capital only if the unit is named after a person; no plural symbols, no full stop, a space after the number; do not mix names and symbols; one prefix only, joined to the unit; products with a space, quotients with a negative power or one solidus.
- **Prefixes (atto to tera):** atto $10^{-18}$, femto $10^{-15}$, pico $10^{-12}$, nano $10^{-9}$, micro $10^{-6}$, milli $10^{-3}$, centi $10^{-2}$, deci $10^{-1}$, deca $10^{1}$, hecto $10^{2}$, kilo $10^{3}$, mega $10^{6}$, giga $10^{9}$, tera $10^{12}$. The kilogram is the only base unit with a prefix.

key_terms.definition_md: The unit of one of the seven base quantities of the SI.

A name or symbol placed before a unit to multiply it by a power of ten.

sections.heading: 3. Practical units; measuring length, mass and time
sections.body_md:
- **Light year:** distance light travels in a year, $2.998 \times 10^{8}\times 3.156 \times 10^{7} \approx 9.46 \times 10^{15}$ m. **Astronomical unit:** mean Earth–Sun distance, $1.496 \times 10^{11}$ m. **Parsec:** $3.08 \times 10^{16}$ m $\approx 3.26$ ly.
- **Angstrom** $= 10^{-10}$ m; **fermi** $= 10^{-15}$ m; **unified atomic mass unit** $1\ \text{u} = 1.66 \times 10^{-27}$ kg, one twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom.
- **Parallax:** a baseline $b$ subtending a small angle $p$ (radian) at an object gives $D = b/p$. One parsec is the distance at which 1 AU subtends 1 arcsecond ($4.848\times 10^{-6}$ rad).
- **Methods:** lengths by scales, vernier and screw gauge (everyday), electron or X-ray methods (atoms), parallax and radar echoes (Moon, planets, stars). Masses by balances, mass spectrometers (atoms) and orbits (planets, stars). Times by pendulum and quartz clocks, and atomic clocks for the highest precision.
- Worked: a star of parallax 0.4 arcsecond is $1/0.4 = 2.50$ pc $\approx 8.14$ ly away.

sections.heading: 4. Errors, significant figures, rounding off and order of magnitude
sections.body_md:
- **Accuracy:** closeness to the true value. **Precision:** closeness of repeated readings. **Systematic errors** (zero error, faulty calibration, wrong technique, personal habit) shift readings one way; **random errors** scatter them and are reduced by averaging; the **least count** limits a single reading.
- With readings $a_1 \dots a_n$: mean $a_\text{mean}$; absolute error $|\Delta a_i| = |a_\text{mean} - a_i|$; **mean absolute error** $= \sum|\Delta a_i|/n$; **relative error** $= \Delta a_\text{mean}/a_\text{mean}$; **percentage error** $=$ relative error $\times 100\ \%$. Worked: swing times mean 1.86 s, mean absolute error 0.02 s, 1.1 %.
- **Significant figures:** the certain digits plus one uncertain digit. Non-zero digits count; zeros between them count; leading zeros do not; trailing zeros count after a decimal point but not in a whole number without one; powers of ten do not count.
- **Rounding off:** drop digit above 5, raise the last kept digit; below 5, leave it; exactly 5 with nothing after, make the last kept digit **even** (7.865 → 7.86, 7.875 → 7.88).
- **Arithmetic:** add or subtract by the least number of **decimal places**; multiply or divide by the least number of **significant figures**. Exact numbers do not limit the answer. Worked: $21.34 + 3.7 + 0.052 = 25.092 \to 25.1$; $14.2\times 6.35 = 90.17 \to 90.2$; $135 \div 4.2 = 32.14 \to 32$.
- **Order of magnitude:** write $N = a\times 10^{k}$ with $1 \le a < 10$; the order is $10^k$ if $a \le 3.16$ and $10^{k+1}$ if $a > 3.16$. The age of the universe, 4.36 \times 10^{17} s, is of order $10^{18}$ s.

sections.heading: 5. Dimensions and dimensional formulae; principle of homogeneity
sections.body_md:
- The **dimensions** of a quantity are the powers of the base quantities in it; the **dimensional formula** writes them in square brackets: $[F] = [\mathrm{M}\,\mathrm{L}\,\mathrm{T}^{-2}]$, $[E] = [\mathrm{M}\,\mathrm{L}^{2}\,\mathrm{T}^{-2}]$, $[P] = [\mathrm{M}\,\mathrm{L}^{-1}\,\mathrm{T}^{-2}]$, $[G] = [\mathrm{M}^{-1}\,\mathrm{L}^{3}\,\mathrm{T}^{-2}]$, $[h] = [\mathrm{M}\,\mathrm{L}^{2}\,\mathrm{T}^{-1}]$.
- Pure numbers and ratios of like quantities (angle, strain, refractive index) are **dimensionless**.
- A constant takes the dimensions that make its equation balance: from $F = Gm_1m_2/r^2$, $[G] = [F][r^2]/[m^2]$.
- **Principle of homogeneity:** every term on both sides of a correct equation has the same dimensions; only like quantities can be added, subtracted or equated; the argument of sin, log or exp is dimensionless.

key_terms.definition_md: An expression showing the powers of the base quantities that make up a quantity, such as [M L T⁻²] for force.
In a correct physical equation every term has the same dimensions.

sections.heading: 6. Uses and limitations of dimensional analysis
sections.body_md:
- **Checking an equation:** find the dimensions of every term; if they differ the equation is wrong. $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$ and $P = \rho g h$ pass; $K = \tfrac12 mv$ fails.
- **Dimensions of constants:** in $\left(P + a/V^2\right)(V - b) = RT$, $[a] = [P][V^2] = [\mathrm{M}\,\mathrm{L}^{5}\,\mathrm{T}^{-2}]$.
- **Converting units:** $n_2 = n_1\left[\dfrac{M_1}{M_2}\right]^{a}\left[\dfrac{L_1}{L_2}\right]^{b}\left[\dfrac{T_1}{T_2}\right]^{c}$. Examples: $1\ \text{N} = 1.00 \times 10^{5}$ dyne; $1\ \text{J} = 1.00 \times 10^{7}$ erg; $9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2} = 32.2$ ft s$^{-2}$; $G = 6.67 \times 10^{-8}$ in CGS units.
- **Limitations:** it cannot give pure numbers such as $\tfrac12$ or $2\pi$; it cannot handle sin, log or exp of a dimensional quantity or a relation with a sum of terms; a dimensionally correct equation is not necessarily correct; it cannot tell quantities of equal dimensions (work, torque) apart.

notes.exam_tips_md:
- Write units with every number; convert to one system before calculating; round only at the end.
- Unit names and symbols: lower-case names, no plural symbols, no full stops, a space after the number, one prefix only.
- Error questions: mean, then each absolute error, then mean absolute error, then relative and percentage error.
- Add by decimal places; multiply by significant figures; a dropped exact 5 makes the last kept digit even.
- To check an equation, find the dimensions of **every** term; dimensional analysis never gives numerical constants.

cards.front_md: Why must a unit be well defined, reproducible and invariable?
cards.back_md: So that every observer, anywhere and at any time, gets the same number for the same quantity.

cards.front_md: Base units of the CGS, FPS and MKS systems?
cards.back_md: CGS: centimetre, gram, second. FPS: foot, pound, second. MKS: metre, kilogram, second.

cards.front_md: How does MKSA differ from MKS?
cards.back_md: It adds the ampere as a fourth base unit, for electric current.

cards.front_md: Unit of force in CGS, FPS and MKS?
cards.back_md: Dyne, poundal and newton.

cards.front_md: How many dyne make one newton?
cards.back_md: $1.00 \times 10^{5}$ dyne, because $1\ \text{N} = 1000\ \text{g} \times 100\ \text{cm s}^{-2}$.

cards.front_md: Name the seven SI base units.
cards.back_md: Metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin, mole, candela.

cards.front_md: The newton in base units?
cards.back_md: $\text{kg m s}^{-2}$.

cards.front_md: The pascal in base units?
Define the radian and the steradian.
cards.back_md: Radian: angle at the centre subtended by an arc equal to the radius, $\theta = s/r$. Steradian: solid angle subtended by an area $r^2$ of a sphere, $\Omega = A/r^2$.

cards.front_md: Is it correct to write "5 kgs." ?
cards.back_md: No: symbols are not pluralised and take no full stop. Write 5 kg.

cards.front_md: Is the unit name "Newton" written correctly?
cards.back_md: No: names of units are written in lower case, newton; only the symbol N is a capital.
Atto, femto and pico.

cards.front_md: Prefixes for $10^{9}$ and $10^{12}$?
cards.back_md: Giga and tera.

cards.front_md: Which SI base unit has a prefix in its name?
cards.back_md: The kilogram.

cards.front_md: Value of a light year?
cards.back_md: About $9.46 \times 10^{15}$ m: speed of light × one year.

cards.front_md: Value of an astronomical unit and of a parsec?
Values of the angstrom and the fermi?
What is the unified atomic mass unit?
cards.back_md: One twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom, $1\ \text{u} \approx 1.66 \times 10^{-27}$ kg.

cards.front_md: State the parallax relation for distance.
cards.back_md: $D = b/p$, with the baseline $b$ and the parallax angle $p$ in radian.

cards.front_md: How is the mass of an atom measured?
cards.back_md: With a mass spectrometer, in unified atomic mass units.

cards.front_md: Systematic versus random errors?
cards.back_md: Systematic errors shift every reading the same way; random errors scatter readings and are reduced by averaging.

cards.front_md: Define the percentage error.
cards.back_md: $\dfrac{\Delta a_\text{mean}}{a_\text{mean}} \times 100\ \%$, with the mean absolute error $\Delta a_\text{mean} = \sum|\Delta a_i|/n$.

cards.front_md: Rule for adding and subtracting measured values?
cards.back_md: Keep the least number of decimal places.

cards.front_md: Rule for multiplying and dividing measured values?
cards.back_md: Keep the least number of significant figures.

cards.front_md: Round 7.865 to 3 significant figures.
cards.back_md: The dropped digit is exactly 5 and the last kept digit 6 is even, so 7.86.

cards.front_md: Find the order of magnitude of a number.
cards.back_md: Write $a \times 10^{k}$ with $1 \le a < 10$: the order is $10^{k}$ if $a \le 3.16$, otherwise $10^{k+1}$.

cards.front_md: Dimensional formula of force and of energy?
cards.back_md: $[\mathrm{M}\,\mathrm{L}\,\mathrm{T}^{-2}]$ and $[\mathrm{M}\,\mathrm{L}^{2}\,\mathrm{T}^{-2}]$.

cards.front_md: State the principle of homogeneity.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) The parallax p of a star is the angle subtended at the star by the baseline b, and D = b/p with p in radian. (b) D = 1 ÷ 0.25 = 4.0 pc. In metre, D = 4.0 × 3.08 × 10¹⁶ = 1.23 × 10¹⁷ m. In light year, D = 1.23 × 10¹⁷ ÷ 9.46 × 10¹⁵ ≈ 13.0 ly.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Systematic errors push every reading the same way; causes are a zero error and a faulty scale. Percentage error = 0.012 ÷ 2.06 × 100 ≈ 0.58 %.
